analysis.one_liner: Repeals Depression-era limits on utility holding companies, replacing them with lighter regulator access to company records.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 never got a committee vote, dying after one July 1999 hearing with 30 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tear down the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, a New Deal law that restricts how utility holding companies are organized and what they can own, and replace it with a lighter system where federal and state regulators can demand company books and records only to the extent they matter for utility rates. It hands oversight from the Securities and Exchange Commission to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and lets FERC exempt companies and transactions it deems irrelevant to rates. The bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Utility holding companies and their affiliates, which would be freed from the 1935 Act's structural restrictions on how they organize and what they may own. They would remain subject to regulator access to records tied to utility rates, but with a new, narrower framework and a broad FERC exemption authority.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electric and gas utility holding companies

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 and replaces it with the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1999 [S2][S3].

Gives FERC and state commissions access to the books and records of holding companies, affiliates, and associates, but only where the records are relevant to costs that show up in utility rates [S2][S3].

Requires FERC to exempt holding companies that exist only because they own qualifying facilities, exempt wholesale generators, or foreign utility companies, and authorizes FERC to exempt any person or transaction whose records it finds irrelevant to jurisdictional rates [S2][S3].
Moves oversight from the SEC to FERC, transfers related records, and gives FERC Federal Power Act enforcement powers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Utility ratepayers, who would rely on a weaker oversight regime: the 1935 Act's structural limits on holding companies disappear, and the replacement lets FERC exempt companies and transactions it finds irrelevant to rates, narrowing what regulators can look at.

drawbacks.text: The bill directs FERC to exempt holding companies built around qualifying facilities, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility companies, and lets FERC exempt any person or class of transactions it finds irrelevant to jurisdictional rates, which narrows regulators' visibility into exactly the affiliated companies whose costs can end up in ratepayer bills [S2][S3].

Repealing the 1935 Act removes its structural limits on how utility holding companies are organized, so companies can combine utility and non-utility businesses under one roof; consumers' only protection becomes records access for rate purposes, and the bill limits state access to records identified in a pending proceeding and subject to trade-secret safeguards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a real deregulation win for utility holding companies, dressed with genuine but narrower ratepayer protections: regulators keep records access tied to rates and keep authority over whether affiliate costs can be charged to customers [S3]. But the protections are weaker than what they replace, the new exemption authority can shrink them further, and the 1935 Act's structural limits on holding-company organization simply disappear. Consumers bear the downside; holding companies get the flexibility.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1999, sent to the House Commerce Committee, referred to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and got one subcommittee hearing, but never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on June 25, 1999 by Rep. Tauzin with 21 other original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Commerce [S1][S5].
Referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power on July 13, 1999, which held a hearing on July 22, 1999 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a subcommittee or full committee vote and was never reported to the House floor before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric and gas ratepayers kept the stricter 1935 Act oversight, since the deregulation never advanced, while utility holding companies remained under the existing rules they had sought to escape. Nobody gained new ground; the status quo held.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ratepayers, who kept the stricter 1935 rules

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship skewed Republican, 22 of 30, but the bill had Democratic support including original cosponsor Rep. Towns, and no vote ever occurred to reveal a full partisan split.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utility holding companies
industries.note: Repealing the 1935 Act frees holding companies from structural limits on how they organize and what they can own, letting utility and non-utility businesses mix under one roof. Ratepayers' only remaining protection is narrower records access tied to rates, with broad FERC exemption authority that can shrink it further [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Qualifying facilities, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility companies
industries.note: The bill requires FERC to exempt holding companies that exist solely to own these entities from records-access requirements, removing even the replacement law's light touch on them [S2][S3].
The SEC loses its PUHCA oversight jurisdiction; the bill transfers the related records and functions to FERC [S2][S3].

FERC becomes the permanent federal gatekeeper over holding-company records and exemptions and gains Federal Power Act enforcement powers, giving it a central ongoing role in a lighter regulatory regime [S2][S3].
